title: Fair housing safe listing descriptions on Mac: a realtor checklist before you publish
metaTitle: Fair Housing Safe Listing Descriptions for Realtors on Mac
description: Write listing copy that describes the home, not the buyer. Learn the risky wording, free checks, a review routine, and where Lazur helps on your Mac.
intro: Fair housing safe listing descriptions describe the home, its features, and its location. They do not describe the buyer, the family, or who a property is good for. This page shows what that looks like, what mistakes can cost you, and a review routine you can run this week.
tldr: Fair housing safe listing descriptions talk about the home and the location, not the buyer or the family.
Risk often hides in friendly phrases like 'perfect for a young couple', so read for meaning, not only for banned words.
Most agents review their own copy, so a second reader and a dated review log do most of the practical work.
No tested study shows which checks reduce violations, so treat every fix as a habit you can explain, not a guarantee.
Lazur can explain and point at wording on your Mac, but it does not decide what is compliant.

blocks.text: What fair housing safe listing copy looks like

A safe listing describes the property. It names the rooms, the features, the condition, and the nearby places a buyer can reach. It does not say who should live there, who should skip it, or what kind of family fits best. That line is the whole idea behind this page.

Use a simple test on every sentence. Ask whether it tells a buyer about the home or about a type of person. 'Open kitchen with a gas range' describes the home. 'Perfect for a young couple' describes a person. The first line is fine to publish. The second needs a rewrite before it goes live.
This test is a habit, not a legal ruling. It helps you catch wording that deserves a second look. It does not tell you how a regulator would judge your copy, so check your brokerage rules for that.
Why friendly listing copy creates fair housing risk

Most agents do not write discriminatory copy on purpose. The risk usually comes from habit. Phrases like 'great for families,' 'exclusive area,' or 'walk to the church' sound warm and normal. They can still steer a buyer toward or away from a neighborhood or a group.

Research shows the problem can hide in plain sight. A 2020 study in Social Forces looked at Seattle rental ads. It started with 278,005 Craigslist ads posted from March 2017 to September 2018. After removing near-duplicates, 45,358 listings remained.

The authors found a pattern. Listings in predominantly White neighborhoods leaned on trust and neighborhood history and culture. Listings in non-White neighborhoods leaned on incentives, transportation, and development features. None of that needed the word race to show up.

That is the core problem for a word list. A list finds words. The authors argue this kind of racialized discourse appears without any explicit mention of race, so a keyword check would miss it. Your review has to read for meaning as well.
The wording that most often needs a second look
No list is complete, and no list settles a question. Still, the same groups of wording come up again and again. Treat them as prompts to read closer, not as a verdict on any one phrase.

items: Household fit: phrases such as 'perfect for young professionals' or 'ideal for a couple' describe the buyer, not the home.
Religion and community: a nearby church, a faith group, or a community label can read as steering.
Neighborhood character: words like 'exclusive,' 'safe,' or 'up and coming' are judgments about an area, and they can carry coded meaning.
Ability and access: describe the feature plainly, such as a level entry or stairs, and avoid claims about who can or cannot use it.
Area-based incentives: check whether incentive or transportation language shows up in some neighborhoods more than others across your listings.

blocks.text: If a phrase fits more than one group, rewrite it. A rewrite costs a little editing time, and it is usually worth it.
What fair housing complaints look like and who handles them

NFHA's 2025 Trends Report, covering 2024, found disability-based discrimination made up the majority of filed complaints, at 54.59%. That share matters for access language. Describe features plainly, and avoid claims about who can use a home.
Private nonprofit fair housing organizations processed 74.12% of complaints in that report. HUD handled 4.85%. In practice, most complaints were processed by local nonprofits, not by HUD.
NLIHC's summary calls the report a record for complaints. It does not give a total count, so this page does not give one either.
What a listing mistake can cost you

Start with time. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says about 55% of real estate brokers and 54% of real estate sales agents are self-employed. If you are one of them, no compliance department reviews your copy. You do that work yourself, on your own schedule.

The median pay for the job was $57,400 per year in May 2025. BLS projects 2% growth in jobs from 2025 to 2035, which is slower than the average for all occupations. Review time is part of the work you already do, so its cost hides inside your week.

The cost of an actual violation is harder to pin down. I found no public figure for fines, lost listings, or complaint outcomes tied to listing copy. This page does not invent one. Ask your broker and your state real estate regulator what applies to you.

A complaint can also pull you into a process you did not plan for, even when you did not mean harm. Good records and a review habit help you explain your process. They do not make a complaint go away on their own.

blocks.text: Checks you can run without buying anything
You do not need new software to start. These checks use tools you already have on your Mac and in your inbox.

items: Read the draft out loud once. Your ears catch words about people that your eyes skip.
Highlight every word that describes a person, a family, or a group. Delete it or move it to a feature.
Check every mention of a school, church, shop, or neighborhood label. Keep only facts you can state plainly.
Compare the draft against the property facts sheet. If a line is not a fact about the home, cut it.
Send the draft to a second reader, such as your broker or a colleague, and ask them to point at wording.
Save the final text with the date and the reviewer's name.

blocks.text: A worked example: fixing one listing draft

Here is a sample draft. 'Perfect for a young couple who want a quiet, safe neighborhood. Great for families with kids. Walk to the church on the corner.' Read it with the test from earlier, one sentence at a time.

Three lines need work. 'Perfect for a young couple' describes a buyer. 'Great for families with kids' does the same with a household type. 'Walk to the church' points to religion. 'Quiet, safe neighborhood' is a judgment about the area, so replace it with a fact you can point to, such as the street type.

The rewrite uses facts: 'Open kitchen with a gas range. Fenced backyard and bedrooms on one floor. Park and bus stop across the street.' Every line now describes the home or the location. None describes a buyer.
Notice what changed. The rewrite gives a buyer more concrete facts, not fewer. The copy still sells the home. It just stops telling anyone who fits.

blocks.title: Keep a review log
blocks.text: Keep a simple log with the date, the listing address, the phrases you changed, and who reviewed the final text. If a question comes up later, the log shows what you checked. Store it where your brokerage says client records belong.
Where Gmail and Google Sheets fit your review routine
Gmail and Google Sheets are not compliance tools. They help you send drafts for review and keep a record of changes. Used together, they give you a paper trail you can search.

In Gmail, turn on templates for the review request you send most. Go to Settings > See all settings > Advanced, then enable Templates. Write one short request that asks a second reader to flag wording about people. Use the same request every time.

Apple's Text Replacements save approved phrasing you reuse. Go to Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Add a short shortcut and the full neutral line, such as one about parking. Text Replacements only speed up typing. They do not check your copy.
For the log, make one Google Sheets tab called Review log. Use four columns: date, listing address, phrase changed, and reviewer. Filter by address when a question comes up later.

Common mistakes realtors make with listing review

items: Checking only for obvious words. Coded language can appear with no race term at all.
Treating a banned-word list as a pass. A list finds words, not meaning or context.
Approving your own copy with no second reader, then publishing the same day.
Reusing an old listing line without rereading it. Old wording can carry old habits.
Pasting client details into an AI tool. Follow your brokerage's rules on client data first.
Skipping the record. If you cannot show your process, you cannot show that a review happened.

blocks.text: A simple habit fixes most of these. Read for meaning, get a second reader, and save what you changed. Each step is small, and none of them needs new software.

faq.question: Is a fair housing safe listing description the same as a legal compliance check?
faq.answer: No. It is a writing habit and a review routine. A legal read depends on current rules, your state, and your brokerage. Ask your broker or an attorney for that answer before you rely on any checklist, including this one.

faq.question: Can I still use words like quiet or family-friendly?
faq.answer: Ask what the word describes. Quiet can describe a street, but it can also judge an area. Reviewers often read family-friendly as a comment on who fits. Rewrite both with facts about the home or the street.

faq.question: Does Lazur check my listing for fair housing violations?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can read what is on your screen, explain a phrase out loud, and circle it. It is not a compliance checker. I found no study that tests whether AI or word-list checkers reduce violations.

faq.question: Do realtors have to complete fair housing training?
faq.answer: NAR says REALTORS must complete Fair Housing / Anti-Bias Training when they become members and every 3 years after. The requirement began January 1, 2025, with a deadline of December 31, 2027. Check your own status with NAR or your board.

faq.question: Is a word list enough to catch problem wording?
faq.answer: No. A 2020 study of rental ads found coded neighborhood language that never named race. The authors argue keyword checks would miss it. Read each line for meaning, then use a list only as a prompt.

faq.question: Can I paste a client's details into an AI tool to help with a draft?
faq.answer: Not until you check your brokerage's rules on client data. Remove names, phone numbers, and private facts from the draft first. Use only the property details you need for the wording.

faq.question: Where should I keep my review log?
faq.answer: Store it where your brokerage says client and listing records belong. A Google Sheet is easy to search, but confirm your brokerage policy before you use it for records.

faq.question: Can Lazur set up Gmail templates for me?
faq.answer: Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not click for you. Ask it to walk you through Settings > See all settings > Advanced, and do each click yourself.

costs.title: Review time comes out of your week
costs.text: BLS says about 55% of brokers and 54% of sales agents are self-employed. That means the review work often lands on you alone. Nobody checks the copy unless you set up that step. Time spent reviewing is time you are not showing homes.

costs.title: Complaints mostly go to nonprofits first
costs.text: NFHA's 2025 report says private nonprofit organizations processed 74.12% of complaints, versus 4.85% by HUD. A complaint can reach a local group before anyone at a federal office. You may spend time answering questions about listing copy, even when you did not intend a problem.

costs.title: Mandatory training has deadlines
costs.text: NAR says REALTORS must complete Fair Housing / Anti-Bias Training when they join and every 3 years after. The requirement began January 1, 2025, with a deadline of December 31, 2027. Missing a deadline is a cost you can avoid with a calendar reminder.

costs.title: The price of a violation is unknown
costs.text: I found no public figure for fines, lost deals, or complaint outcomes tied to listing copy. That gap matters. Ask your broker and state regulator what outcomes apply in your market, and do not rely on numbers from vendor blogs.

causes.title: Friendly phrases feel harmless
causes.text: Most listing phrases about families, neighborhoods, or community come from a warm instinct. They sound like good marketing. That is why they slip past a quick read. The habit is the cause, not bad intent, and it needs a deliberate review to catch.

causes.title: Coded language avoids race words
causes.text: A 2020 study of Seattle rental ads found that listings in predominantly White neighborhoods leaned on trust and neighborhood history. Listings in non-White neighborhoods leaned on incentives and transportation. None of it needed a race term, so the pattern is easy to miss.

causes.title: Word lists check words, not meaning
causes.text: A banned-word list can flag one term and pass a sentence that means the same thing. The study authors argue that racialized discourse appears without any explicit mention of race. A list alone cannot read context, so it cannot settle the question.

causes.title: No compliance team and no second reader
causes.text: With most agents self-employed, the person who writes the copy often approves it too. Nobody else reads it before it goes live. Errors that a second reader would catch then reach buyers and sellers unchanged.

causes.title: Old copy and templates get reused
causes.text: Agents reuse last year's listing lines, open house flyers, and social posts. Old wording carries old habits. A line that passed review once may not fit a new listing, and nobody rereads it when it is pasted into a template.

fixes.title: Describe the home, not the buyer
fixes.text: Rewrite any line that describes a person or household as if it were a feature. Replace 'perfect for a young couple' with a fact about the home, such as an open kitchen or a fenced yard. Keep the copy warm, but let the warmth come from specifics. This is practitioner guidance, not a tested method.

fixes.title: Run a read-for-meaning pass
fixes.text: Read each sentence and ask whether it describes the property, the location, or a type of person. A word list only finds words. A meaning check catches the coded phrases a list misses. Read the draft out loud once as well, because it helps you hear wording you skim past.

fixes.title: Get a second reader before publishing
fixes.text: Ask your broker or a colleague to read the final draft and point at wording. Use a Gmail template for the request so it takes less effort each time. Ask for flags, not approval, so the decision stays with you and your brokerage.

fixes.title: Keep a dated review record
fixes.text: Log each listing with the date, the address, the changed phrases, and the reviewer. Store the log where your brokerage says client records belong. A record shows your process. It does not prove that the copy was compliant.

fixes.title: Save approved phrasing for reuse
fixes.text: Use Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements to store neutral lines your broker has already reviewed. If you use Lazur, you can also save them as snippets. Reuse only wording you have checked against the current listing.

fixes.title: Check the rules from the source
fixes.text: Read NAR's fair housing pages and your state's rules before you trust any checklist, including this one. NAR says REALTORS must complete Fair Housing / Anti-Bias Training when they join and every 3 years after. Your state regulator and your broker set the rules you must follow.

fixes.title: Use AI for reading, not judging
fixes.text: Ask an AI assistant to explain a sentence or suggest neutral alternatives. Do not ask it to certify a listing. I found no study that tested whether AI or word-list checkers reduce violations, so verify each change yourself before you publish.

fixes.title: Remove client details before any AI tool
fixes.text: If you paste a draft into an AI tool, remove names, phone numbers, and private client facts first. Follow your brokerage's rules on client data, and read the tool's data policy before you use it for listing work.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Set up your review log
plan.text: Create a Google Sheets tab called Review log with date, listing, phrase changed, and reviewer. Confirm with your brokerage that the sheet is an approved place for listing records before you enter real addresses.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Write down your wording groups
plan.text: Copy the groups from this page into one note: household fit, religion, neighborhood character, ability and access, and area incentives. Keep the note open while you edit drafts.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Reread your most recent listings
plan.text: Pull up the copy from your latest listings in Gmail or your listing tool. Mark any phrase about a buyer, a household, or a group. Rewrite each one with a feature or a location.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Get a second reader
plan.text: Send each new draft to your broker or a colleague in Gmail before it goes live. Use your saved template for the request. Ask them to point at wording, not to approve it for you.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Save the final versions
plan.text: Log each final text with the date and reviewer. Save approved neutral lines in Apple Text Replacements or as Lazur snippets, so the same wording comes back next time.
